title: Three perfect days in London: fireworks, poppies and Istanbul
dek: A Remembrance weekend in London: Westminster on a wet Friday, the northern heights and Ally Pally's fireworks on Saturday, and the Cenotaph and the V&A's new Istanbul show on Sunday.

hero.caption: The Palace of Westminster. On Sunday morning the city falls silent at the Cenotaph, a few hundred metres up Whitehall.

intro:
This is the weekend London does its two big November rituals back to back. Bonfire Night falls on Thursday, and the large ticketed fireworks displays fill Saturday night. At Alexandra Palace there's a drone show and a bonfire. Blackheath and Battersea Park light up the south. On Sunday morning the National Service of Remembrance is held at the Cenotaph on Whitehall. The two-minute silence starts at 11 a.m., and veterans march past for about half an hour afterwards.

The plan works around both. Friday stays indoors in Westminster and Trafalgar Square, which is the right call: the forecast has rain arriving in the afternoon. Saturday heads up to Hampstead and Highgate for the Heath, an old pub lunch and a Victorian cemetery. It ends on Ally Pally's hilltop, which has the best view of any fireworks in town. On Sunday, watch the Remembrance service from the pavement on Whitehall, then walk west through the parks to South Kensington. The V&A's **Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires** opens there on Saturday, and it's the big new exhibition of the autumn.

Expect cool, cloudy days around 9–10°C, darkness before half past four, and pubs with the fires lit. One thing to know: the Lord Mayor's Show isn't this weekend. In 2026 it's on Saturday 14 November, so the City stays quiet.

days.title: Friday: Westminster and Trafalgar Square
days.intro: A rainy-day plan with roofs over everything: the Abbey in Remembrance week, a long lunch in an old library, and the National Gallery's Friday late.

stops.name: Regency Café
stops.text: This black-tiled 1940s caff is a five-minute walk from the Abbey, and it's one of the best plain breakfasts in London. Order a full English with bangers, a mug of tea and toast. It closed at the end of 2024 and reopened in summer 2025 under Fevzi and Zafer Gungor, who kept it as it was. Expect to share a table. Check the day's hours before you go, and go early: the queue for lunch starts around 12:30.

stops.name: Westminster Abbey
stops.text: Come when the doors open at 9:30. In November the Abbey shuts to visitors in the early afternoon, and the crowds build quickly in Remembrance week. Inside the west door is the Grave of the Unknown Warrior, the only tomb in the church you're asked not to walk on. Then see the coronation chair and the Lady Chapel's fan vault. Adults pay £32 and you should book ahead. If you want more, the hour-long *War and Remembrance* tour runs at 1 p.m. on Friday, costs £42 with admission and takes 15 people.

stops.name: The Cinnamon Club
stops.addr: Old Westminster Library, 30-32 Great Smith Street, SW1P 3BU
stops.text: Since 2001 this modern Indian restaurant has filled the Grade II-listed Old Westminster Library, and the books still line the walls of the main room. It's where Westminster comes for a long lunch, The cooking is refined rather than fiery, and spice is used carefully on game and seafood. Lunch is served from noon to 2:30 p.m. and it's expensive. Book ahead.

stops.name: National Gallery
stops.text: Walk up Whitehall to Trafalgar Square. The National Gallery is free and stays open until 9 p.m. every Friday, so you don't have to rush. Choose a few rooms rather than trying to see everything: the Van Eyck *Arnolfini Portrait*, Velázquez's *Rokeby Venus*, Turner's *Fighting Temeraire* and Van Gogh's *Sunflowers*. Leave your umbrella at the cloakroom. Its next big show, *Van Eyck: The Portraits*, opens on 21 November.

stops.name: Gordon's Wine Bar
stops.text: Down a few steps off Villiers Street are candlelit vaults that have been a wine bar since around 1890. The Gordon family has run it since the 1970s. Order a glass of sherry or Madeira from the long list, with a plate from the cheese counter. You can't book for small groups, so on a wet Friday arrive by half past five to get a table.

stops.name: Rules
stops.text: Thomas Rule opened an oyster bar on Maiden Lane in 1798. Its red banquettes and walls of cartoons and portraits still look the part. November is game season, so order grouse or pheasant if they're on, or the steak and kidney pudding. In *The Sunday Times*, Camilla Long called the duck rillettes "gamey, spicy, fabulous". Rules is grand rather than fashionable, and that's what makes it fun on a dark night. Book, and expect a discretionary service charge on the bill.

days.title: Saturday: Hampstead, Highgate and Ally Pally
days.intro: A day on the northern heights: the Heath in the morning, an Elizabethan inn, Highgate's cemetery, then fireworks from the hill at Alexandra Palace.

stops.name: Ginger & White
stops.text: Take the Northern line to Hampstead. Its lifts take you up from London's deepest Tube platform. Ginger & White is a few steps away, down the lane at Perrin's Court. Order free-range eggs on sourdough, a flat white, and a slice of cake to take onto the Heath. It's small and fills up by mid-morning on weekends, so if you arrive before ten you'll get a seat by the window.

stops.name: Hampstead Heath and Parliament Hill
stops.text: Walk east past the ponds to the top of Parliament Hill. From there the whole skyline lies to the south, with St Paul's, the Shard and the City towers lined up under the clouds. Then turn north across the open heath and through the woods to Kenwood. The walk takes about 45 minutes. Paths get muddy after Friday's rain, so wear proper shoes.

stops.name: Kenwood House
stops.text: This neoclassical villa on the Heath's northern edge holds the Iveagh Bequest. It includes Rembrandt's late *Self-Portrait with Two Circles*, Vermeer's *The Guitar Player* and a fine room of Gainsboroughs. It's a short, very good visit, and Robert Adam's library is the room to linger in. Entry is free, but English Heritage recommends booking a time for the house. Check the day's opening hours when you book.

stops.name: The Spaniards Inn
stops.text: This 1585 inn is ten minutes' walk west of Kenwood, beside the old tollhouse that still narrows the road. Keats and Dickens are among its claimed regulars, and so is the highwayman Dick Turpin. Sit in the wood-panelled rooms by the fire. Order the wild boar and ale sausages with English mustard, the scotch egg with beetroot piccalilli, or the crab thermidor on toast, which The Infatuation picked out over the mains. Book for Saturday lunch.

stops.name: Highgate Cemetery
stops.text: A 210 bus or a 30-minute walk along the Heath's edge brings you to Swain's Lane. From November to February the cemetery opens daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and last entry is at 3:30, so don't linger over lunch. The East Cemetery has Karl Marx's huge bronze head and George Eliot. In the West Cemetery, the Egyptian Avenue and the Circle of Lebanon look their best in the low autumn light. Book ahead, and leave if a funeral is taking place.

stops.name: The Flask
stops.text: Walk up the hill to Highgate village, where this Grade II-listed Fuller's pub has a plaque reading "The Flask 1663". It has a famous old servery with glazed sash windows, and its cellars are linked to Dick Turpin. Have a pint of London Pride or ESB, then stay for an early dinner, since the kitchen serves until 10 p.m. on Saturdays. You'll want to leave by about 7 to get to the fireworks.

stops.name: Fireworks & Drone Festival at Alexandra Palace
stops.text: Ally Pally sits on a ridge a couple of miles northeast of Highgate, so its fireworks rise over the whole of London. Saturday is the grown-up night. The gates open at 4 p.m., and there's a bonfire, a funfair, street food, a German bier festival and ice skating. The fireworks and drone show starts at 8 p.m., and Eats Everything plays a DJ set afterwards. Tickets start from £11.50 and should be bought in advance. Light rain is forecast for the evening, so bring a hood.

days.title: Sunday: Remembrance, the parks and South Kensington
days.intro: Breakfast on Piccadilly, the silence on Whitehall, a long walk west through three royal parks, then a roast and the V&A's new Istanbul exhibition.

stops.name: The Wolseley
stops.text: The Wolseley serves breakfast from 8 a.m. on Sundays in a 1920s car showroom turned Viennese-style grand café, with black lacquer and a vaulted ceiling. In January Time Out ranked it London's best breakfast, calling it "always-fun and always-busy". Order the kedgeree, the omelette Arnold Bennett or a grilled kipper with mustard butter. Book the first sitting so you can be on Whitehall by half past nine.

stops.name: National Service of Remembrance at the Cenotaph
stops.text: Whitehall opens to the public at 8 a.m., and space on the pavements is limited, so come early. You don't need a ticket. At 11 a.m. guns on Horse Guards Parade mark the two-minute silence. Then come the wreaths and the Royal British Legion's march past, which lasts until about 11:25. Big screens stand along the street. Leave large bags at the hotel, since police search everyone, and don't take photos during the silence.

stops.name: St James's Park to Kensington Gardens
stops.area: St James's Park and Hyde Park
stops.text: Once the crowds thin out, take a royal park walk. Head across St James's Park past the pelicans, up through Green Park to Hyde Park Corner, then along the Serpentine. The trees will be close to their best colour. Leave the park at the Albert Memorial and walk down Exhibition Road. Allow about an hour. Great George Street stays closed for the service, so cross into St James's Park by Horse Guards Road or Storey's Gate.

stops.name: Anglesea Arms
stops.text: This is a proper Sunday-lunch pub on a quiet terrace south of the station, with a wood-panelled dining room. OpenTable diners keep mentioning the big Yorkshire puddings and generous slices of roast beef. The Beef Wellington is the other dish people talk about. Book a table, since Sunday lunch here gets full. If you've walked from Whitehall, it's also a good place to dry off and sit by the fire.

stops.name: Constantinople to Istanbul at the V&A
stops.text: On its second day, the V&A's new show traces one city across 1,600 years and two empires in more than 200 objects. They include the tenth-century ivory Veroli Casket, Gentile Bellini's 1479 portrait of Mehmed II, a 17th-century Ottoman processional scroll and Osman Hamdi Bey's *Ladies Taking a Walk*. Weekend tickets are £27, and the exhibition is in galleries 38 and 39. The museum is free and open until 5:45 p.m., so leave time for the cast courts and the café's tiled rooms.

stay.name: The Goring
stay.text: London's royal favourite is still led by Jeremy Goring. The Princess of Wales stayed here the night before her wedding. It has 69 rooms, a large private garden behind the hotel, and a Dining Room that had a £2.5 million refit in 2024. From Victoria it's a short walk to the Abbey, Whitehall and the Wolseley, which makes it well placed for Friday and Sunday morning.

stay.name: The Kensington
stay.text: This hotel fills a row of white Regency townhouses on Queen's Gate. It has 150 rooms, three drawing rooms off the lobby, and a clubby panelled bar. It's a short walk from South Kensington station and the V&A, so Sunday finishes on your doorstep. From Gloucester Road and South Kensington, the District and Circle lines run straight to Westminster.

stay.name: hub by Premier Inn London Westminster St James's Park
stay.text: The rooms are compact, starting at 11 square metres. They're well designed, with good showers, air conditioning and touchscreen room controls. The location is hard to beat this weekend: St James's Park station is next door, and the Abbey, Whitehall and the Regency Café are all a few minutes' walk away. Some rooms face a light well instead of a window, so ask when you book.

events.name: Pitchfork Music Festival London: The Avalanches
events.text: The Australian sample collagists headline a Friday of the week-long, multi-venue festival. Elsewhere that night, Olof Dreijer plays the ICA. On Saturday Noname headlines the Roundhouse and there's a Dalston venue takeover. On Sunday Hania Rani plays the Royal Festival Hall.

events.name: Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires opens
events.text: Opening day of the V&A's major exhibition on Byzantine and Ottoman Istanbul, with more than 200 objects. It runs until 9 May 2027. Tickets are £25 on weekdays and £27 at weekends.

events.name: Arsenal v Hull City
events.text: A Premier League afternoon in north London. Fulham host Newcastle at Craven Cottage at the same time. On Sunday at 2 p.m., Crystal Palace play Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

events.name: Alexandra Palace Fireworks & Drone Festival
events.when: Sat. gates 4 p.m., fireworks 8 p.m.; Sun. family display 6 p.m.
events.text: London's biggest Bonfire Night weekend has a bonfire, a drone show, a funfair, a German bier festival and a DJ set from Eats Everything on Saturday. Sunday is an earlier, family-focused show. Tickets start from £11.50.

events.name: Blackheath and Battersea Park fireworks
events.text: These are south London's two big council displays. Both have funfairs. IanVisits lists adult tickets at £16 for Blackheath and £18 for Battersea, which also runs on Sunday.

events.name: National Service of Remembrance
events.when: Sun. Whitehall opens 8 a.m.; silence at 11 a.m.
events.text: The nation's main act of remembrance, with the two-minute silence, wreath-laying and the veterans' march past, which ends around 11:25. Anyone can watch from the pavements, and you don't need a ticket.

know: **From Heathrow (LHR):** the Heathrow Express runs non-stop to Paddington every 15 minutes and takes about 15 minutes. Advance singles cost from £10 if booked 30 days ahead. The Elizabeth line is cheaper and slower, taking about 27 minutes to Paddington, with trains every 10 minutes, and it runs on through Bond Street, Tottenham Court Road and Farringdon. A black cab usually takes about an hour.

**From Gatwick, City, Stansted and Luton:** the Gatwick Express takes about 30 minutes to Victoria, which is handy for the Goring. London City is on the DLR. The Stansted Express runs to Liverpool Street. From Luton, a shuttle takes you to Luton Airport Parkway for Thameslink trains to St Pancras.

**Pay as you go:** tap a contactless card or phone, or an Oyster card, when you go in and when you come out. Use the same card or phone all day, so the daily cap applies: £8.90 for zones 1–2 and £16.30 for zones 1–6 since March 2026.

**Engineering works:** the Tube lines are clear this weekend. On the Overground, the Mildmay line has no service between Willesden Junction and Clapham Junction on Saturday and Sunday. The Suffragette line is closed between South Tottenham and Barking Riverside until Tuesday 10 November. Neither affects this plan.

**Remembrance Sunday:** Whitehall and Parliament Street fill with spectators from 8 a.m. Great George Street is closed, and Westminster and Charing Cross stations are very busy before and after the service. Westminster Abbey isn't open to sightseers on Sundays.

**Fireworks night:** expect crowded trains toward Alexandra Palace, Blackheath and Battersea Park on Saturday evening, roughly 6–8 p.m. and again after 9 p.m. Allow extra time, and buy tickets in advance, since gate prices are higher.

**Weather and light:** the forecast is 9–10°C and cloudy. There's rain on Friday afternoon, a little on Saturday evening, and Sunday should be mostly dry. Sunset is before 4:30 p.m., so do outdoor things in the morning.

**Tipping:** many restaurants add a discretionary 12.5% service charge, and if it's there you don't need to tip again. In pubs you order at the bar, and nobody expects a tip. The Lord Mayor's Show is next Saturday, 14 November, not this one.
